one_liner: Small MIT Linux libc; in one zig-built run its atoi (2.3x) and sprintf %f (1.2x) beat glibc, strtod loses 4.3x.
what_it_does: musl is a complete ISO C99/POSIX 2008 C library for Linux, the libc behind Alpine images, zig cc's *-linux-musl targets and many static binaries. You do not add it for one function: you pick it as the target libc, usually linked statically, and atoi, strtol, strtod and the printf family keep their standard signatures, so code compiles unchanged. kraj/musl is Khem Raj's downstream GitHub mirror (default branch kraj/master carries Yocto-style patches on top of upstream; VERSION reads 1.2.6, tagged 2026-03-20).
how_it_is_fast: atoi is a 16-line loop (skip isspace, read a sign, accumulate 10*n - digit as a negative int) with no errno, locale or range handling, while glibc 2.35's atoi is a call to strtol(nptr, NULL, 10). strtok/strtok_r have the same strspn-then-strcspn structure as glibc, but musl's strspn and strcspn special-case a one-character separator set (a byte loop, and __strchrnul's word-at-a-time HASZERO bit trick), which is cheap for the benchmark's 4-byte average tokens. printf %f goes through fmt_fp, which converts the value to x87 long double and expands it into base-1e9 uint32 limbs, emitting 9 digits per limb; why that edges glibc by 1.18x was not established from the sources read. The losses have visible causes: strtod's __floatscan returns early only for short integer-like inputs and otherwise rescales a base-1e9 big number in 2^29 steps (the benchmark's '123.123E-4' style inputs take that path), and every printf call runs printf_core twice (a validation pass with f=0, then the output pass).
when_to_use: Your build already targets musl (Alpine containers, zig cc -target x86_64-linux-musl, static Rust or Go binaries) and a hot path parses short decimal integers with atoi: 3.96 vs 9.28 ns per call on 1-5 digit strings.

Tokenising with strtok or strtok_r on a single-character separator and short tokens (CSV-like lines): 4.94 vs 14.76 ns per token, even though each 185-token line also pays for a 985-byte strcpy, where musl is the slower libc.
Fixed-precision %f formatting of small doubles where the libc choice is already musl: 136 vs 161 ns per sprintf("%.6f").
You want readable, MIT-licensed reference code to copy for a single routine (atoi.c is 16 lines, floatscan.c about 500) rather than LGPL glibc code.
when_not_to_use: Parsing doubles: musl's strtod was 4.3x slower than glibc's (226.72 vs 52.40 ns); a dedicated parser such as fast_float is faster still.
Integer and mixed printf formatting: sprintf("%d") 1.21x slower and a four-conversion snprintf 1.44x slower than glibc; use {fmt}, jeaiii/itoa or std::to_chars instead of switching libc.
As a general speed upgrade: glibc won 20 of the 32 rows, including 32-byte malloc/free (11x), qsort (2.8x), regexec (5.9x) and strtod; musl+jemalloc closes the malloc gap only.
Validating untrusted numeric input with atoi: musl computes in int with no overflow check or errno, so out-of-range strings hit signed overflow; use strtol and check errno and the end pointer.
Code that depends on glibc behaviour (NSS modules, GNU extensions, locale data) or on glibc-tuned SIMD string routines.

integration.form: static lib (libc.a; a shared libc.so that is also its own dynamic linker is built too)
integration.dependencies: none beyond the Linux syscall API; building needs GNU Make and a freestanding C99 compiler with gcc-style inline asm, weak aliases and hidden visibility (INSTALL)
integration.min_toolchain: C99 compiler (GCC, clang, cparser and PCC have built it); use a musl-targeted toolchain, the musl-gcc wrapper, or zig cc -target *-linux-musl (the benchmark used zig 0.15.2)
integration.platforms: Linux only: i386, x86_64 (x32 experimental), ARM, AArch64, MIPS, MIPS64, PowerPC, PowerPC64, S390X, SuperH, Microblaze, or1k, RISC-V 32/64, LoongArch64 (INSTALL)
integration.thread_safety: strtok keeps a static pointer (use strtok_r); atoi, strtol, strtod and snprintf are reentrant; stdio FILE operations lock per stream
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial: same ISO C/POSIX API as glibc, so number parsing and formatting calls compile unchanged, but switching means changing the whole libc target (allocator, locale, NSS and static-linking behaviour change with it)

gotchas: What was measured is zig 0.15.2's bundled musl, not this repository: a pre-1.2.6 copy (its fmt_fp still declares the long-double-sized stack buffer that upstream shrank in August 2024). Zig overrides strlen, strcmp, strncmp and strcasecmp (lib/c/string.zig) and memcpy, memmove, memset and memcmp (compiler_rt), but its lib/c/stdlib.zig exports only abs, labs and llabs, so the atoi, strtod, printf, bsearch, strtok and strrchr rows do run musl C code.

Harness flaws: each row is one calibrated sample (the loop stops once a run exceeds 62.5 ms of the 250 ms target; no repetitions), the glibc build calls libc.so through the PLT while musl is linked statically, and under -O3 the glibc build's stdlib.h pulls in the extern-inline bsearch from bits/stdlib-bsearch.h (__USE_EXTERN_INLINES), so the 1.5x bsearch row probably compares a compiler-inlined copy against musl's library loop (inference, not disassembled). The strtok rows charge a 985-byte strcpy per 185 tokens to each libc.
musl's atoi has no overflow handling: 10*n - digit is computed in int, so inputs beyond the int range are undefined behaviour and differ from glibc's strtol-based result (C leaves both undefined).

Upstream commit f96e47a (2025-07-02) introduced a buffer overflow in floating-point decimal formatting that 0ccaf05 fixed on 2025-09-19; the fix says no release carried it, but a git snapshot of master or kraj/master from that window does, so pin a tag such as v1.2.6 rather than an arbitrary mirror commit.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Only when the libc choice is already musl for deployment reasons: for parsing doubles fast_float beats glibc's strtod 3-5x (and glibc beat musl 4.3x here), and {fmt}, Ryu or Dragonbox format doubles about 16-26x faster than sprintf, far beyond musl's 1.18x edge.
verified_claims_summary: fereidani/musl-vs-glibc built one C file with zig 0.15.2 (clang 20.1.2, -O3 -march=native -flto=full) for the host's dynamic glibc (Ubuntu 22.04, probably 2.35) and zig's bundled static musl and ran each row once on an AMD Ryzen 7 PRO 5850U (2025-11-18). In the number rows musl won atoi (3.96 vs 9.28 ns over 512 strings of 1-5 digits) and sprintf %.6f (136.34 vs 160.56 ns) but lost strtod (226.72 vs 52.40 ns), sprintf %d (44.83 vs 36.91 ns) and the snprintf mix (250.64 vs 174.18 ns); across all 32 rows musl was faster in 9, slower in 20 and tied in 3.
status_note: Upstream musl is actively maintained (v1.2.6 tagged 2026-03-20, upstream fixes through September 2026) and kraj/master was last updated 2026-09-28, but kraj/musl is a downstream mirror and the only evidence is one unrepeated third-party run of zig's bundled musl with no musl-specific benchmark in the repo; MIT, so single files are easy to copy.
